Affaires sensibles est l'émission quotid: Affaires sensibles is France Inter's daily show, launched in autumn 2014 and hosted from day one by Fabrice Drouelle. Every afternoon, a major case, mostly from the 20th century: crimes, yes, but also industrial disasters, health scandals, espionage, trials that changed the law, affairs of state. Chernobyl, the Rainbow Warrior. More than ten years later, the catalogue is approaching 3,000 episodes.
La forme tient en deux temps. D'abord un: The form comes in two parts. First, about forty minutes of storytelling: INA archives, real voices from the time, film music, razor-sharp editing — the early seasons even had actors play some scenes. Only then, an interview with someone who knows the case: a journalist, lawyer or historian. The show has been adapted into a book, for the stage and on France 2, co-produced with the INA.
Le débit, les silences, la façon de pose: The pace, the silences, the way he lays down a proper name like an exhibit on a table. It isn't reading, it's staging — he could narrate a vacuum cleaner manual and you'd wonder whether the vacuum cleaner makes it out alive.
Tout ce qu'on reproche au true crime — l: Everything people hold against true crime — voyeurism, drama turned into entertainment — the show answers through its very structure: the thrill first, the analysis after. You come for the story, you stay for the context.
Archives, documentalistes, montage, un i: Archives, researchers, editing, an expert guest: a documentary a day, five days a week. A costly heritage object that only public service broadcasting can fund.
Premier malentendu à dissiper : Affaires: First misunderstanding to clear up: Affaires sensibles is not a true crime show. It's an audio encyclopedia of the last fifty years, and that's precisely what lifts it above the genre. Where many crime podcasts — including very good ones like L'Heure du Crime — tell a case, Affaires sensibles tells it and then puts it in perspective. You don't leave with a crime story, you leave with History. It's also the show that made Lolo want to do podcasts.
Deux réserves et une demie. Le catalogue: Two and a half reservations. The catalogue is a bottomless pit: nearly 3,000 episodes, and a library without a librarian — the Radio France app offers about twenty themes, covering only a hundred or so episodes. The mechanics show: story, dramatic build-up, cliffhanger before the break, interview — three episodes in a row and you can see the strings. That's the price of a daily show. And the half: the show is so embodied that it's inseparable from its storyteller. To start, scroll the history, pick a case you think you know, and get ready to discover you didn't.
